newsitem.title: CHINA: France says hopes EU arms embargo on China to go.
newsitem.headline: France says hopes EU arms embargo on China to go.

text.p: France hailed Chinese moves towards accepting United Nations human rights standards on Tuesday and said it hoped a European Union ban on arms sales to China imposed after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown could be lifted.

The Paris Foreign Ministry welcomed China's commitment during a visit by French Defence Minister Charles Millon to join a U.N. Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural rights and to study favourably joining a pact on political and civil rights.
"France salutes this decision and will continue its efforts to contribute positively to the gradual consolidation and extension of the rule of law in China," a statement said.

In a thinly veiled attack on European partners who want the European Union to sponsor a U.N. resolution criticising China's human rights record, the ministry said: "This decision is a signal which the international community must not ignore.
"It proves that a constructive, demanding dialogue which bears fruit is preferable to confrontation."
Denmark said on Tuesday it would table a U.N. motion critising China's human rights record despite Beijing's pledge to sign the economic and social rights covenant.
In Beijing, Millon ruled out sales of defence equipment to China in the short term but said he hoped an EU arms embargo would be lifted over time.
He said his visit to China this week had been mainly a political trip, paving the way for a visit by President Jacques Chirac next month.
Possible exchanges in military technology as well as high level visits and the meeting in Beijing of a joint strategic commission had been discussed, Millon told reporters.
All military sales remain banned by the EU since China sent in the army to crush student-led protests for more democracy centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square on June 3-4, 1989.
"I hope and I am confident that in the future, through reciprocal decisions, the situation will change," Millon said.
Asked if France would take the initiative to end the ban, Millon said the embargo had been agreed by all 15 members of the European Union and could only be lifted by a similar consensus.
He said Chinese President Jiang Zemin had raised the issue of human rights in their meeting on Monday.

China's official Xinhua news agency said Jiang praised Paris for its "wise and far-sighted" decision not to co-sponsor a U.N. resolution critical of Beijing's human rights record, hinting that such a move would boost French business with China.
The Chinese president said he had told his advisers to study the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to establish whether it was compatible with China's constitution, Millon said.
Jiang said he hoped France would play a role in persuading more Western countries to avoid confrontation in favour of dialogue, Xinhua reported.

France said last month it would not co-sponsor a motion to criticise China's human rights policies at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva, saying Beijing had made progress on protecting basic freedoms.

The two sides also discussed air control, adding that China had built some 30 airports in recent years, Millon said. He did not comment on whether European consortium Airbus Industrie would win a major order for planes during Chirac's visit.

Industry officials have said Airbus hopes to sell up to 75 airliners to China next month to meet China's rapidly growing demand to boost air travel. Chinese officials have said the order may not be so large.
China bought 30 airliners from the European consortium Airbus Industrie in April last year in a $1.5 billion deal signed during a visit to France by Premier Li Peng.
